statement: The prototype shall demonstrate that MDOT can bring in multiple streaming data sources.

The system shall use confidence in the data, severity of the condition, and confirmation by another source as factors for determining whether an insight should move from awareness to a recommended action.
The system shall promote a connected-vehicle insight from awareness to a recommended action when it aligns with traffic sensors, weather data, or a field report and crosses an operational threshold.
The system shall require human review before dispatching crews or changing traffic control.
The system shall treat strong corroboration, clear impact, and sufficient urgency as the boundary for issuing a recommendation rather than only an alert.

Connected-vehicle data shall be considered to add enough value for a recommendation when it shows a broader or earlier pattern than the fixed sensors and that pattern is consistent over a short period rather than a single spike.
Connected-vehicle data shall be treated as especially useful when sensors are sparse or when the event is unfolding upstream before the fixed equipment catches it.
The system shall prefer the fixed-sensor view when it is clearly available, stable, and directly measuring the condition of interest.
Connected-vehicle insight shall supplement or accelerate the decision and shall not override a solid sensor-based picture unless there is a clear reason to do so.
The system shall alert when a feed stops arriving.
The system shall alert when a feed slows down unusually.
The system shall alert when a feed starts repeating messages.
The system shall alert when feed timestamps are clearly out of sequence.
The system shall trigger a check when bad values fall outside expected ranges or do not make sense in context.
Alert severity should be based first on operational impact.
The system should suppress or downgrade an alert when the feed is a known test source.
The system shall keep an alert suppressed as long as an explicitly expected condition remains valid.
The system shall escalate an alert if a known nuisance pattern changes into something operationally significant.
The system shall provide a clear way to re-arm suppression when the risk changes, because suppression is not permanent.
The system shall show how the system resolved the conflict or built the combined record.

The system shall retain derived outputs for a shorter period for day-to-day operational use.
The system shall delete or purge data sooner if the data is duplicated.

The system shall purge duplicates.
The system shall purge any data that exceeds the approved retention window.
Legal, contractual, and public-record requirements shall override the default purge timing and be enforced separately.
Pooled or shared vehicles should be treated as separate vehicle records when they can be distinguished.
Trailers and power units should be represented separately when possible.
The system should track each part of a trailer and power unit combination independently when possible.
When a vehicle unit is temporarily unavailable, the system should keep the vehicle entity and mark its status as inactive, offline, or unavailable instead of deleting it.
Vehicle-derived events such as hard braking, sudden deceleration, and probe-speed observations should usually be stored as separate observations linked back to the vehicle.
Storing vehicle-derived events as separate observations linked to the vehicle should support traceability and reuse of raw event data later.
The traveler record shall remain canonical around the identity that can be reasonably maintained.
Changes to traveler attributes such as home area, commute pattern, or user status shall be treated as time-stamped updates rather than as new people.
If a traveler is no longer active, the system shall keep the record for historical analysis and mark it inactive instead of creating a duplicate.
If traveler subtypes are used, the system shall separate travelers by role or usage pattern only when that separation matters operationally.
The system shall support subtype separation for examples such as commuter, occasional traveler, and freight-related traveler behavior.
The system shall not split the same person into multiple records solely because the person's attributes changed.
When identity is uncertain, the system shall preserve prior history and link the new observation carefully rather than overwrite the old record.
Users should receive very short, task-focused training on how to read provenance, confidence, timestamps, and conflict indicators.
Users should receive examples of when to trust an output and when to verify it.
Users should receive quick-reference guidance for the main use cases, including incidents, winter operations, and traveler messaging.
The interface should be understandable with minimal training on day one.
Day-one onboarding should consist of a basic orientation and a handful of guided scenarios rather than a long course.
If users cannot become productive quickly, the views should be simplified instead of requiring them to learn a complex workflow upfront.
Users should be taught to trust an output when the data is recent, the provenance is from a known high-quality source, the confidence is high, and the indicators all agree.

Users should be taught to verify an output when the timestamp is stale, the source is weak or missing, the confidence is low, or there is a conflict between vehicle, roadway, weather, and traveler signals.
Users should be taught that incident situations are exception cases.
Users should be taught that rapidly changing winter weather is an exception case.
Users should be taught that sensor outages are an exception case.
Users should be taught to verify before acting when there is a conflict and a safety or operational action depends on it.
The view is too hard if users cannot reliably complete the main task after a short orientation.
Repeated help requests are an indicator that the view is too hard.
Frequent misinterpretation of the same fields is an indicator that the view is too hard.
Users ignoring the provenance and confidence cues and making mistakes from that is an indicator that the view is too hard.
If a user needs coaching every time to find the same answer, the view should be simplified.
If the workflow takes so many steps that people stop using it for routine work, the view should be simplified.
For a prototype, the complexity should be reduced rather than forcing users to learn around a confusing design.
Users shall verify outputs when there are major construction changes.
Users shall verify outputs when there are special events.
Users shall verify outputs when traffic patterns are unusual enough that historical assumptions no longer work.
Users shall verify outputs when there are multi-source conflicts.
Users shall verify outputs when one source says conditions are normal and another source shows a sudden spike or drop.
Users shall verify outputs when the data is incomplete.
Users shall verify outputs when there is a long gap in timestamps.
Users shall verify outputs when the result is based on a model estimate rather than direct observation.
Users shall verify outputs when the consequence of acting on a bad output is high.

If an output will drive an operational decision with safety impact, congestion impact, or public messaging impact, and any of those warning conditions are present, the output must be verified immediately before action.
A confident-looking output must be verified if it depends on older data, a single source, or a model estimate during a fast-changing situation.
Verification is required when a result seems unusually clean compared with surrounding conditions, because that may indicate a bad feed or a stale update.
Confidence alone is not sufficient if the context suggests the answer could have changed since the last update.

The prototype should not add many extra data intake channels unless they clearly support core safety use cases, traffic management use cases, asset management use cases, winter operations use cases, or planning use cases.

Users should stay in the existing process whenever the task is routine, local, or already well covered by a current operational system.

The prototype should take over when it can show a clearer combined picture faster than the current process.
The prototype shall include a feed only when it changes a real decision the user would otherwise make with less confidence or more delay.

The prototype shall include a feed when it improves timeliness.
The prototype shall include a feed when it reduces uncertainty.

The system shall prioritize translating the condition that most changes the immediate action first.

When two conditions are both important, the system shall prioritize the condition that is less visible or more likely to be misunderstood without the system’s help.
For the prototype, the system shall be available essentially all the time during normal operating hours.
For the prototype, the system shall target uptime in the high nineties.
Planned interruptions shall be acceptable only for maintenance or upgrades.

The system shall keep using the last trusted value only for a very short time when a source is unavailable.
If an outage lasts beyond the short window, the system shall remove the source from the operational picture.
If an outage lasts beyond the short window, the system shall either switch to another trusted source or present the gap openly instead of pretending the data is still valid.
For intermittent source failures, the system shall use a degraded mode in which the source is quarantined from the general feed until it proves stable again.
The system shall generate an informational alert when a feed issue is minor, short-lived, or self-correcting and does not affect the operational picture.
The system shall generate a warning when a feed is delayed, partially missing, or flaky enough that staff should pay attention but can still rely on the rest of the system.
The system shall generate a critical alert when a feed is down, when the data is clearly stale beyond the acceptable window, or when missing data could change an operational decision.
The system shall avoid alerting on feeds that are not operationally relevant at that moment.
If a feed is still usable but delay meaningfully weakens confidence, the system shall treat the condition as at least a warning and keep the feed in the picture only with a stale indicator.
If new wording does not change reporting, controls, or how people act on the data, the system should usually adopt the new wording right away and retire the old term in the next update.
If the old wording is still embedded in existing reports, contracts, or historical outputs, the system should keep both the old and new wording in parallel for a while.
A change to the wording should be blocked or delayed if a provider agreement, external standard, or internal governance rule says it cannot be redefined unilaterally.
The system shall keep the old term in parallel until the last important consumer has been updated and there is no reasonable chance of confusion in active use.
The system shall allow some reports or contracts to move to the new wording sooner.
The retirement point for the old term shall be driven by the slowest required dependency.
If leadership decides the old term can be preserved only in archived history, the system shall follow that decision.

The system shall provide short help text or tooltips.
The system should support very short, task-based training rather than a long classroom session.
The system should include built-in guidance.
The system should provide sample views.
The system should provide a quick reference guide or cheat sheet for the most common tasks.
The system should follow standard accessibility expectations.
The system should not rely on color alone to convey information.
The system should provide text labels, patterns, or icons in addition to color, especially on maps and dashboards.
The system should provide readable contrast.
The system should support scalable text.
The system should provide clear focus states.
The guided first-run walkthrough shall point out the main screens and the most common actions.
The guided first-run walkthrough shall avoid overwhelming users.
In fast-moving situations, updates should feel near real-time.
The system should refresh high-priority operational data every few seconds to around a minute, depending on the source.
Heavier summaries or planning views may refresh more slowly.
The prototype system shall handle many data streams at once without slowing down the displays that users rely on most.
The prototype system shall scale up cleanly as more data sources are added.
The system shall fail gracefully when a data feed goes down.
The system shall provide a simple fallback view or cached recent data for critical events so operators can still make decisions until the feed is restored.
The system shall provide basic redundancy for important parts, especially components that receive, store, or serve live data, so that one failure does not take the whole system down.
The system shall queue or buffer incoming data when possible.
The system shall provide clear monitoring and alerting for support staff so they know quickly when something is wrong and can intervene before users are impacted.
The transition to the operational product shall be phased rather than implemented as a single cutover.
The prototype shall run in parallel with existing workflows before users are moved to the operational product.
The system shall validate outputs before users are moved over.
Migration shall preserve historical data and key configurations.
The switch to the operational product shall be scheduled and communicated carefully to avoid disrupting daily operations.
The system shall support a controlled rollout starting with a small group of pilot users before broader launch.
The migration process shall include training for staff.
The migration process shall include clear cutover dates.
The migration process shall include a rollback plan in case something critical does not work as expected.
The system shall handle differences in timestamps across data feeds.
The system shall handle differences in location references across data feeds.
The system shall handle differences in field definitions across data feeds.
The system shall use strong mapping rules and validation checks to catch mismatches early during data conversion.
The system shall provide reconciliation reports during migration to compare old and new outputs and identify gaps before go-live.
The system shall support a staged transition from the prototype to the operational system.
The system shall avoid changing users' day-to-day processes all at once.
The new system shall fit into existing workflows as much as possible.
The new system shall replace existing workflow steps only after they have been proven stable.
The migration process shall include close communication with agency staff.
The system shall provide a very simple feedback path for pilot users.
The system shall support a dedicated contact or ticket process for pilot users to report issues.
The project team shall triage problems quickly during the pilot.
Each reported item shall have a clear owner.
During the pilot, the team shall use short review cycles to fix and retest issues quickly before they reach a wider group of users.
Training should be role-based.
Training should address the different ways operators, analysts, and managers use the system.
Training should be hands-on.
Training should use real examples from traffic, weather, and incident situations.
Training should not consist only of a slide deck.
The system rollout should include quick reference materials.
The system rollout should include follow-up support after go-live.
The system shall continue processing incoming data even if one feed goes down.
The system shall provide basic redundancy for the most critical components.
The system shall run duplicate instances of critical ingestion and processing components in separate environments or nodes so that one instance can take over if another fails.
The system shall queue incoming data when a downstream component is unavailable.
The system shall automatically fail over for the most important functions.
The system shall provide near real-time alerts for ingestion delays.
The system shall provide near real-time alerts for abnormal data volumes.
The system shall provide dashboard views showing system health.
The system shall provide dashboard views showing backlog status.
The system shall provide dashboard views showing whether data is current by source.
The system shall route alerts to the appropriate support staff.
If a data quality issue is severe, the system shall suppress the output rather than risk misleading users.
Alerts shall be prioritized by impact.
Issues that affect live outputs shall escalate immediately.
Routine warnings shall be sent to the operations team first.
Critical failures shall notify the system owner right away.
